title: Savoir and connaître
why: English has one verb “to know”; French has two. This lesson teaches savoir for facts and skills and connaître for people and places, with a simple test to choose between them, and finishes the work on can started in the previous lesson.

Two verbs for “to know”

English has one verb, “to know”. French has two, and they're not interchangeable: savoir is for what you know in your head (facts, information, skills); connaître is for what you've met or experienced (people, places, works).

savoirconnaître
jesaisconnais
tusaisconnais
il, elle, onsaitconnaît
noussavonsconnaissons
voussavezconnaissez
ils, ellessaventconnaissent
  • The singular forms of savoir all sound the same and rhyme with mais; the plural uses another stem, sav-.
  • Connaître has a circumflex on the î before a t: connaître, il connaît. Since a 1990 spelling reform, il connait without the accent is also accepted, but you'll mostly see the traditional spelling. In the plural, -ss- appears: nous connaissons.
Je connais Julie, mais je ne sais pas où elle habite.I know Julie, but I don't know where she lives.

Je ne sais pas (I don't know) is one of the phrases you'll hear most. In casual speech it shrinks to je sais pas, or even “chais pas”. Understand them, but write je ne sais pas.

", "

Savoir: facts and skills

Use savoir for information. It's often followed by que (that), si (if, whether), or a question word: où, quand, comment, pourquoi, à quelle heure.

FrenchEnglish
Je sais que tu es fatigué.I know (that) you're tired.
Tu sais si le musée est ouvert ?Do you know if the museum is open?
Vous savez où est la gare ?Do you know where the station is?
Elle sait quand le train part.She knows when the train leaves.
Je sais la réponse !I know the answer!

As with dire, English can drop “that”, but French always keeps que.

Savoir + infinitive: a skill

Savoir + infinitive means “to know how to”, and it's how French says “can” for a skill you've learned:

Je sais nager, mais je ne sais pas conduire.I can swim, but I can't drive.
Tu sais cuisiner ?Can you cook?

Compare Je sais nager (I know how to swim) and Je peux nager (I'm able or allowed to swim right now: the pool is open, my arm is better). English says “can” for both; French separates them. And never “je sais comment nager”: the infinitive follows directly.

", "

Connaître: people, places, works

Connaître is always followed by a noun: a person, a place, a book, a movie, a restaurant. It means “to know” in the sense of “to be familiar with”, “to have been there”.

Tu connais Bordeaux ? — Non, mais je connais bien la Bretagne.Do you know Bordeaux? — No, but I know Brittany well.
Nous connaissons un très bon restaurant à Lyon.We know a very good restaurant in Lyon.

The quick test

  • A person or a place after the verb → connaître: Je connais Marie, Je connais Marseille.
  • que, si, où, quand or an infinitive after the verb → savoir: Je sais où elle habite, Je sais nager.

Regions of France

Regions take la or l' and, like feminine countries, en: la Bretagne (Brittany, en Bretagne), la Provence (en Provence), l'Alsace (en Alsace), la Normandie (Normandy, en Normandie).

Tu connais ? on its own is a very common way to ask “Have you heard of it? Have you been there?” Answer Oui, je connais ! or Non, je ne connais pas. And “Do you know Paul?” is always Tu connais Paul ?, never “tu sais Paul”.
